newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Pope to bring unity message to secular Czechs.
newsitem.headline: Pope to bring unity message to secular Czechs.

text.p: Pope John Paul was beginning a visit to the Czech Republic on Friday, bringing a message of European and Christian unity to a highly secular society where few people ever attend church.

The 76-year-old Pontiff, on his third trip to Prague since the 1989 fall of communism, plans a mass for young people to commemorate the 1,000th anniversary of the martyr's death of a Czech saint who took the gospel to Poland.
He will also join other church leaders in ecumenical worship.
"The majority of our Czech nation is looking forward with some hope to the visit of Pope John Paul," said Miloslav Fiala, spokesman of the Czech Catholic Bishops' Conference.

But a February survey by the Centre for Empirical Studies, a polling agency, found just 37 percent of respondents believed in God and that among people aged between 18 and 29 only 28 percent were believers.
A separate survey showed just six percent went to church every week while 54 percent never attended a service.

The Czech Republic, with one of the highest standards of living in the former East bloc, has a long tradition of secularism, dating back centuries to wars for religious supremacy and further enforced by 50 years of communism.
"There is a tension between the Catholic Church and part of the Czech nation," said Fiala.

The Church is still trying to secure the return of property lost when the communists were tightening their grip on power after World War Two. The Pope may discuss the issue in Sunday talks with Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, who has said he wants it resolved, Fiala said.

Vast crowds greeted the Pope on his first trip to Prague as Pontiff in 1990, when he hailed the fall of communism. Fewer people turned out last time, in 1995, when he canonised Jan Sarkander, tortured to death by Protestants in 1620.
Some Protestants say Sarkander was a traitor who encouraged a Catholic invasion of Czech lands.
However, more than 100,000 are expected to attend each of two open air masses which the Pope, whose health has been fragile in recent years, will hold this time.
President Vaclav Havel, a former dissident playwright seen by many as the leading moral authority in the nation, will greet the Pope on his arrival at 6 p.m. (1600 GMT).

Pope John Paul travels on Saturday to the town of Hradec Kralove, 100 km (60 miles) east of Prague, to mark the 1,000th anniversary of the death of St Adalbert, or Vojtech in Czech, who is seen by Catholics as a symbol of European unity.
He holds another mass on Sunday at Prague's Letna Plain, the scene of Soviet-era military parades and later of huge anti-Communist demonstrations in the 1989 "Velvet Revolution".
As always on papal tours, security is expected to be tight. More than 1,000 police and 250 soldiers are expected to be on duty in Prague.
